text: Day one. The owner hands you the office keys and a folder labelled “Everything Is Bad.” It's as thick as a brick. Where do you start?
The guard won't let you in: “Crisis manager? We've been saved like that three times already.” Your pass isn't ready. How do you get in?
The chief accountant shows you the statement: cash for exactly two payrolls. “That's the good news. The bad news is on page two.” Turn the page?
right: Coffee and a deep breath first

text: The former director's assistant asks whether to keep his motivational posters. One says “Crisis Is Opportunity.” Take them down?
The CFO brings three cash forecasts. Each shows a different debt figure, all equally terrifying. Which one do you trust?
The shop floor chief shows you a machine that “works as long as nobody touches it.” Nobody has touched it since spring. What now?
At your first team meeting everyone stares at the table. Only the intern asks: “So are you going to fire us all?” How do you answer?
The steel supplier calls on your first day: “You're the new one? Great. We've been owed since March.” He sounds exactly like someone owed since March.
right: Ask for a week to dig in

text: 9 p.m. You're still in the office and have only reached the “Really Bad” section of the folder. Dinner is waiting at home. Keep reading?
The night watchman sees your light and brings tea: “The last rescuers left at six. Maybe you'll stick around?” Chat with him?
The company lawyer opens with: “Good news, there are only nine lawsuits.” He's saving the bad news for after lunch. Hear it now?
The warehouse keeper gives you a tour: half the space is full of kettles nobody buys, the other half is empty because the right stock never came. Start where?
right: Order the right stock on credit

text: Your first week's calendar was planned to the minute by the old assistant. The “lunch” slot says “meeting with creditors.” Rearrange it?
Sales shows you their funnel: lots of leads on top, almost nothing at the bottom. The head of sales calls it “an inverted pyramid of success.”
right: Ask for three ideas by Friday

text: HR brings the staffing chart. There's a post called “Deputy for Strategic Optimism.” Someone is on payroll for it, but nobody has seen them.
The family chat asks: “So how was day one? Saved them yet?” You're still in a taxi, unsure you even saved lunch. What do you reply?
right: Call and vent for a bit

text: On his way out the sysadmin says: “Our server is older than half the staff. If I call at night, that's it.” Give him your personal number?
The previous director emails: “Don't judge me too harshly. The password to everything is the company's founding date.” Passwords must change. When?
The bank manager calls at 8:05: “We'd like to understand your plan.” You have no plan yet, only the “Everything Is Bad” folder. What do you say?
right: Improvise a plan on the spot

text: The marketer wants an urgent logo refresh: “New start, new look!” There's no money for logos, or for kettle ads either. Your call?
right: Let them sketch it for free

text: The canteen cook asks if lunches are about to be cut. About ten people in the queue behind him are listening very closely.
The shareholders want a “short rescue plan” by Monday. Short, they explain, means “about forty pages.” You've been here three days.
The evening shift says the heating has been broken since last winter. It's autumn now. There's no money for repairs, but enough for blankets.
At home the cat sits on your laptop, blocking the debt report. He has the exact stare of the chief accountant. Maybe he's right?
Morning inbox: 214 unread, 38 titled “URGENT,” and one titled “not urgent but very important.” Which first?
The process engineer says the defect rate is 12%, “but 2% on paper.” The paperwork was adjusted to avoid upsetting the old director. What now?
A courier brings three boxes of unpaid bills from a mailbox nobody opened for six months. The boxes are labelled in marker: “Later.”
The warehouse keeper whispers about “off the books” stock: a batch of toasters that isn't in any system. The toasters are lovely, though.
right: Find out where they came from

text: Your gym coach texts that you've missed three sessions. “A crisis is no excuse,” he adds. He hasn't met this crisis.
11:40 p.m. Your phone buzzes: “Shop 2: line stopped.” A minute later: “OK, running.” Then: “Stopped again.” Drive over?
right: Let the shift handle it overnight

text: The secretary asks how to sign memos: “Crisis Management” or just “The Directorate.” The first sounds a lot scarier.
Logistics reports three trucks waiting at a client's gate. The client won't unload until an old debt is paid. The trucks are billing like taxis.
The auditor politely asks why the same company car is listed three times. Nobody seems to have seen the car even once.
A foreman with thirty years here brings a notebook: “Everything the old directors wouldn't listen to.” It's written in tiny handwriting.
right: Ask him to talk you through it

text: A rival director “bumps into” you at a café and offers to buy your warehouse “as a friend.” The price is friendly, mostly to him.
In the evening the head of sales asks to give 40% off “just to sell something.” Shipping is tempting, but the margin will cry.
Your pillow says it's missed you two nights running. The debt spreadsheet says the same. Who wins?
The press officer reports a local business site ran “Company Has a Month to Live.” Clients are calling to ask if it's true.
Your deputy suggests starting every day with a 7:30 a.m. briefing “for energy.” Nobody, including you, is feeling energetic.
The landlord reminds you of three months' unpaid rent and offers to “solve it” with a move to the basement. It's “cosy,” he says.
Accounting finds a five-year prepaid subscription to a yachting magazine. The company has no yacht. Not yet, anyway.
A major client invites you in and says at the door: “I'm leaving you, but our coffee is good.” Try to keep them?
right: Let them go, enjoy the coffee

text: The team started a chat called “What Happens Next?” By evening it has 400 messages of rumours. You haven't been added. Ask to join?
right: Let them vent on their own

text: The taxi driver hears where you work: “Oh, the kettle people? Mine's lasted forty years!” You want to hire him for sales.
The shop floor chief asks for new gloves: the old ones are “held together by goodwill.” There's money for half the shift.
The alarm goes off at six. A meeting with creditors is already running in your head, four hours early. Get up and work?
A finance intern finds an error in a contract that could save a million. He says it quietly, like he's apologising. What do you do?
left: Praise him in front of everyone

text: The chief engineer proposes moving two shops onto one schedule to save on power. People would have to switch shifts.
A journalist wants comment on the morning article by 8 p.m. The press officer drafted three versions, from “all great” to “yes, it's tough.”
At home, the fridge holds only ketchup and a yoghurt with your name on it. It's nearly older than your contract.
The CFO offers a “simple fix”: cut a third of the staff and the numbers work. You suspect they only work in the spreadsheet. Your answer?
Facilities finds the company pays for forty parking spaces. Staff own nine cars. The rest are used by the car dealer next door.
Accounting brings the subscription list: seven video-call tools, three note apps and one for “executive meditation.”
The shop chief suggests switching off the lights at lunch. Good savings, but everyone eats right there by the machines.
A logistics staffer proposes a four-day week at lower pay, same workload, so nobody gets laid off.
The lobby coffee machine broke. Its lease costs as much as a car. A real one. Repair it or return it?
left: Return it, use our own kettles

text: Procurement has bought printer cartridges from a friend at triple market price for five years. “But he's reliable,” they say.
The IT director begs you not to touch the server budget: “Save here and lose everything there.” He points at the window for “there.”
The shareholders ask why the savings plan has no layoffs. “Everyone else does it,” they write.
HR suggests freezing hiring and not replacing people who leave on their own. A year's savings without a single dismissal.
Marketing pleads to keep advertising: “Stop talking about ourselves and we'll be forgotten.” Ads are the second-largest cost.
The lawyer finds a lease for a warehouse unused for two years. It can be cancelled, but with a penalty.
The company driver asks if he'll stay. There's one car, and only the old director used it, and he's gone.
The warehouse keeper suggests selling old kettles to staff at cost. Space freed, people happy.
right: Sell to a dealer in bulk

text: A sales rep admits to taking company-paid taxis to clients because “it's awkward to pitch on the subway.”
You're going over the cost list. The last line is your own bonus, already promised by the owner.
left: Waive it for the team fund

text: The watchman notices heaters glowing in empty offices every night. People have been forgetting to switch them off for a year.
Staff bring a box of savings ideas. Inside are 80 notes, from “turn off the printer” to “sell the office ficus.”
Rumour has it the office ficus is worth a month of rent. People want to sell it. It gazes at you with its leaves.
The packaging supplier will cut prices 15% if you order a year ahead. You don't have a year's money.
At the cost-cutting meeting everyone proposes cuts in other departments. Their own are, somehow, the most essential.
Sales wants to keep a trade show in another city. Stand, flights, hotel. It promises “new connections.”
An ex-colleague offers you a job “at a calm company where everything's fine.” Better pay. You've been here two weeks.
Accounting is staying until nine reconciling expenses. You can send them home or stay together and order pizza.
The plastics supplier shows up in person and sits in reception: “I'm not leaving until you pay.” He's brought a thermos and sandwiches for the whole day.
The chief accountant asks who to pay first: the power company, the plastics supplier or the rent. There's money for only one.
The steel supplier proposes a deal: he keeps shipping, you pay him a share of sales. Sounds generous. The share is less so.
The power company sends a notice: disconnection for debt in 10 days. There's a smiley in it, presumably to soften the blow.
The treasurer suggests a “trick”: pay every supplier a little so nobody gets upset. Most likely everybody will.
The kettle lid supplier writes politely: “We understand your difficulties. But lids aren't free.” Not one threat. It's almost awkward.
right: Reply and ask for a month

text: The bank agrees to a short loan but wants “something valuable” as collateral. By inventory, the most valuable item is that ficus.
The steel supplier issues an ultimatum: money by Friday or shipments stop. The line would halt on Monday.
left: Find the money at any cost

text: A retail chain owes you almost as much as you owe everyone else. They've been “about to pay” for four months.
The glass supplier offers a payment delay if you write a nice review for his website. His glass really is good.
The CFO suggests delaying payroll a week to cover a supplier. “Nobody will notice,” he says. Everyone will.
right: Delay it and say so openly

text: Logistics found a carrier at half the price. One catch: delivery is “around the right day, give or take.”
The handle supplier wants twenty kettles “for the family” in exchange for a delay. Must be a big family.
The chief accountant asks if she can come in late tomorrow: it's her third night on the payment calendar.
right: Need you at 9, day off later

text: The plastics supplier is still in reception. Thermos empty, sandwiches gone. Security asks what to do with him.
left: Go out and talk to him

text: You stare at the cash plan: next month's gap is shaped like a cat. The cat is smiling. You aren't.
The steel supplier calls at 10 p.m., not threatening, just tired: “I've got forty people of my own. They need paying too.”
The chief accountant's daughter comes to pick her mum up at 8 p.m. and asks you: “Are you her boss? When will she be home?”
The blender motor supplier proposes barter: motors in exchange for toasters for his canteen.
A creditor will forgive a quarter of the debt if you pay the rest within a week. The only way to find it is selling the warehouse.
A small client will prepay six months if they get 10% off. You needed the money yesterday.
The plastics supplier is back: “Fine, a schedule. But the first payment is tomorrow.” Your calendar already has three other “tomorrows.”
Your sister calls offering to lend “the company” money, since it's so hard. It's just enough for one shipment.
10:15 p.m. Monitoring goes red: the online store is down. Friday night, just when people are choosing kettles for the weekend.
left: Wake up the whole IT team

text: The sysadmin calls at midnight: “The server isn't dead, it's just thinking. For about forty minutes.” Customers say the site looks “sad.”
right: Wait the forty minutes at home

text: Support asks what to tell customers while the site is down: “maintenance,” “we're fixing it,” or the honest “we crashed.”
A developer offers a “quick hack” that'll bring the site back in 10 minutes. What breaks later, he doesn't know. “But something will.”
2 a.m. The site is back. You're in the kitchen wearing one sock, holding cold tea. The team chat is full of fireworks. Now what?
In the morning the sysadmin reports: a cable got “kicked by someone.” There's camera footage. Watch who did it?
The IT director wants a backup server “in case the first one starts thinking again.” There's money, but it's next month's payroll.
A customer writes: “Last night your site took my money but created no order. My cash is somewhere between worlds.” By morning there are thirty such emails.
The sysadmin admits backups were made, but onto the same server. “Saves walking.” The server, remember, likes to “think.”
A cloud provider offers to move everything within a week. Pricey, but you'd sleep well. The migration is its own adventure.
The warehouse software froze, so the keeper is tracking stock on paper. Lovely handwriting, but orders keep coming.
The accounting system says the company has minus seven kettles. Accounting is hunting for where the non-existent kettles went.
An email arrives: “We know your server is weak. Pay and we won't touch it.” Looks like blackmail with typos.
11 p.m. again, red again. This time it's not the site that's down, it's the tool that watches the site. Who watches the watcher?
The on-call developer lost home internet and is fixing the server via phone from the stairwell. Heroism?
left: Send him a taxi to the office
right: Ask him to borrow a neighbour's Wi-Fi

text: 1:30 a.m. While you're on the outage call, the cat walks across the keyboard and posts “zzzzzzzz” to everyone. The sysadmin replies “agreed.”
left: Laugh it off and carry on

text: The night-shift developer asks for a day off after the outage. Another one asks for a day off in solidarity. The site is still shaky.
Customer service wants to give everyone affected a 5% promo code as an apology. The CFO clutches his chest.
The IT director suggests an “incident-free day” celebration with cake. There hasn't been one incident-free day all month.
right: First make it through a day

text: An analyst finds every outage costs as much as a new server. Gorgeous spreadsheet. The server is still old.
An IT contractor offers an “infrastructure audit” for money you don't have. He promises to find “all the bottlenecks.” You already know one.
The sysadmin wants a “Don't Kick the Cables” sign in the server room. He proposes stronger wording. You prefer softer.
Sales complain that while the site was down, rivals sold “our” kettles. They want a lower target as compensation.
While you were saving the site, your nephew's birthday happened. The chat has a photo of the cake: “We saved you a slice.”
The first off-site backup in a year has been running six hours. The sysadmin asks if he can go home and leave it running “on trust.”
7:40 a.m. A business reporter is waiting at the entrance: “Just one question: is the company bankrupt?” It is just one question, but a heavy one.
The press officer brings the morning headlines: “Kettles Cooling Off,” “Will It Boil Again?” and “Who Switched Off Luchik.” Decent puns, honestly.
left: Answer with a pun of our own

text: A popular reviewer posted “Why I'll Never Buy Their Kettle Again.” Judging by the video, his kettle hasn't been cleaned since purchase.
Morning radio invites you on air in half an hour. Topic: “Do crisis managers save companies or just fire people?”
An employee read online that the company is being “sold off in pieces” and asks which piece he belongs to.
left: Explain in person it's a rumour

text: The press team suggests a press conference. Likely turnout: two journalists and one courier at the wrong door.
Local TV wants to film on the shop floor. It's not camera-ready: peeling walls and a “Don't Touch” sign on a machine.
left: Let them film it as is
right: Ask for a week to tidy up

text: A journalist sends questions. Number five: “Is it true the new boss can't work a kettle?” How does he know?
The press officer wants a social media series called “Good News From Us.” So far there's enough for one post. A great post, though.
A rival gave an interview: “We'll gladly take their customers and staff.” Your staff are already discussing it.
A trade magazine wants a column: “Five Lessons From a Crisis.” You've got three so far, and one is “no coffee after six.”
9 p.m. The press team sends tomorrow's article calling you “made of steel.” Right now you'd rather be made of fleece.
A reporter calls in the evening: “The story is running, with or without your comment.” You're at the supermarket checkout.
Your neighbour at the door: “You're the kettle person from the news? Mine leaks, by the way.” She's holding a bag that seems to contain the kettle.
A clip of you saying “A kettle isn't an appliance, it's a mood” hits a hundred thousand views. Half of them are mocking.
right: Get the press team to explain

text: The “kettle as a mood” clip became a meme, and morning sales on the site rose 9%. The press team wants to make it the slogan.
A photographer wants a “confident leader gazing into the distance” pose. The distance outside your window is a garage wall.
left: Shoot on the floor with people

text: The press officer asks whether to tell journalists the exact debt figures. The numbers are scary, but rumours are scarier.
A business podcast invites you to record. The host promises “no tough questions” and, judging by past episodes, is lying.
The team shares yesterday's article: “turns out we're holding up.” Someone asks if it's true.
Quality control reports: in one batch, the kettle lid can pop open at the boil. Six thousand units, already in stores.
The engineer finds the cause: the lid spring was swapped for a cheaper one under the last director. Saved pennies.
right: Look for a cheaper good one

text: The lawyer says legally the recall can take two months. Morally, two weeks would be better.
A store chain asks whether to pull the kettles themselves or wait for your people. Your people are three managers and one van.
The call centre is swamped with recall calls. Four operators, an endless queue. Operator Sveta has lost her voice.
The CFO prices the recall and goes pale. He suggests giving buyers a coupon instead of a refund.
A customer returns a recalled kettle and wants a new one in a different colour, “since you're swapping anyway.” There's no other colour.
The press team argues over wording: “voluntary replacement” or “product recall.” The first sounds softer, the second is more honest.
Three thousand kettles are back at the warehouse. The keeper asks where to put them: the only space left is the old guest dining room.
An engineer proposes not scrapping recalled kettles but replacing the springs and selling them as “refurbished” at a discount.
The evening call centre shift asks for pizza and permission to skip “thank you for contacting us” for the hundredth time.
A message from a stranger: “My kettle's from that batch, the lid popped, but I stepped back in time. Thanks for the warning.”
The engineer wants to stay overnight and test the new spring through a hundred boils. He's already set up a camp bed.
At 10 p.m. the shareholders want a recall report “in two sentences.” You're on your sixth draft of the first one.
Warehouse reports 80% of kettles are back. The other 20% are probably at summer cottages, boiling once a season.
The shop chief suggests an apology edition kettle printed with “Now It Stays Shut.”
QC asks for one more inspector. There's no money for one, but there'd be none for the next recall either.
The supplier of the old, good springs is happy to come back but wants prepayment. “Your predecessors disappointed me,” he writes.
A customer returns her kettle with a pie: “Thank you for being honest. I haven't seen anyone apologise in years.”
The press team wants a short video statement about the recall. Your office lighting makes you look like a ghost.
left: Film on the bright shop floor

text: Among the returned kettles, the watchman finds one with a note: “Please give it back, my grandma gave it to me.” There's a phone number.
11:30 p.m. The owner calls an emergency video meeting “for ten minutes.” You know his ten minutes: an hour and twenty.
The late-night debt meeting is in its second hour. Everyone repeats the same thing in new words. The CFO is sleeping with his eyes open.
left: End it and hand out tasks

text: 12:40 a.m. Your deputy texts: “Awake? I have an idea.” It could be brilliant. Or about the logo.
You're in bed, but the payment table keeps spinning in your head. You're counting columns instead of sheep. The sheep seem offended.
left: Get up and jot it down

text: The CFO texts at 11:10 p.m.: “There's good news, but it can wait till morning. Good night.” Now you'll never sleep.
The emergency night meeting debates whether to call the bank at 7 a.m. Half are for it, half are asleep. Yours is the deciding vote.
6 a.m. You slept four hours. Bank talks today, and your face looks like the company's credit history.
Your deputy proposes a rule: no work messages after 10 p.m. unless there's a fire. He hopes there won't be any fires.
A stress coach, found via an old contract, offers you an hour's chat. That hour is booked by creditors.
Morning: your first run in a month. Five hundred metres in, the phone rings: “The warehouse is flooded.” Just a little.
The night shift fixed the line without you. The shift supervisor is waiting to hear what you'll say.
Your assistant found a 40-minute gap and asks how to fill it: a supplier, the bank, or lunch.
The head of sales notes: “Third day in the same shirt. Is that a strategy?” It isn't.
right: Admit it, go home and change

text: Your fitness band reports: “Today: 312 steps and 41 calls.” Nobody asked it to count calls, but it's trying.
Your country-house neighbour invites you for the weekend: “dig potatoes and don't think.” Sounds like the best crisis plan yet.
Your family suggests a phone-free evening. The phone lies on the table, glaring with a red notification from the bank.
This morning it turns out only the sysadmin has the server room key, and he's on a train till evening. The site works, but prices can't be updated.
The daytime crisis meeting is in hour three. You realise a meeting about cutting costs has eaten half a day's salaries of everyone in it.
right: Sit it out to the end

text: You finally sit down to lunch. A minute later the CFO, the lawyer and the logistics head join you: “Since you're here anyway.”
You leave at 8 p.m. and realise you haven't seen the sun in four days. It's not out now either, but the moon's decent.
The watchman sees you out: “Early today. Eight p.m. is practically morning for you.” He seems pleased.
right: Joke, go back for the laptop

text: At the morning stand-up you ask everyone to name one problem they've kept quiet about. The silence lasts about a fiscal quarter.
Foreman Petrovich admits he trusts no director, but gives you “a C-plus.” This appears to be a compliment.
left: Ask how to earn a B
right: Thank him, get back to work

text: A note in the suggestion box: “Bring back the clean-shop bonus. It was scrapped three directors ago.” It cost next to nothing.
The intern asks if he can stay after probation even though “everything's bad.” He's doing good work.
The sales reps ask you to join a tough client meeting. Not to lead, just “to sit beside us and look important.”
HR proposes an anonymous survey on trust in management. The results could sting. A lot.
Survey results: trust in management is 2.1 out of 10. A comment reads: “The new one at least says hello.” You're the new one.
You eat in the staff canteen instead of your office. Nobody sits at your table. Even the cleaner walks around it.
Workers ask if it's true the new boss is “one of those who come, fire people and leave.”
A young accountant admits she's so afraid of mistakes she enters every transaction three times. Things move slowly.
left: Tell her it's OK to slip

text: The shop chief argues with you in front of everyone and turns out to be right. The whole floor is watching your reaction.
left: Admit it in front of them

text: The head of sales asks you not to impose a “rescue plan” but give him a month for his own. His plan is on a napkin.
You've finally been added to the “What Happens Next?” chat. The first message after: “Shh, the boss is here.” Silence.
A call centre agent is staying late to finish your request. You said “when you have time,” not “today.”
The team suggests a small evening on the shop floor: tea, pie and a guitar. No money needed, just you showing up.
At the shop-floor evening the guitarist hands you the guitar: “The boss sings first. Tradition.” The tradition is three minutes old.
The cleaner asks for a new trolley — she's asked five directors before you. It costs about as much as a café lunch.
right: Add it to the purchase plan

text: By the smoking area, people say you're “alright, maybe, we'll see.” It's the best review of a director in five years.
The chief accountant cracks her first joke in front of you in a month. It's about depreciation. Everyone laughs except the lawyer.
The night foreman texts: “Thanks for coming to the floor yesterday. We'd only ever seen directors in photos.”
The chief accountant walks in without knocking and lays down a statement: for the first time in six months, more came in than went out. By a thousand.
Sales closes their first big deal in three months. The head of sales asks permission to strike the gong. You don't have a gong.
The off-the-books toasters sold out. The warehouse is a third roomier. There's space for a ping-pong table.
The steel supplier unexpectedly sends a card: “Thanks for the first on-time payment. Nobody's treated me this well in ages.”
The site ran a month without a crash. The sysadmin asks if he can now sleep without the phone under his pillow.
left: Yes, and take a day off

text: A lost client is back: “The others had worse coffee, and your kettles are better.” He wants an order with a “welcome back” discount.
The defect rate fell from 12% to 4%. The shop chief wants to hang the chart on the wall. A downward line, finally a happy one.
The bank extended the credit line six months. The bank manager even smiled. Hesitantly, but he did.
right: Plan the next step right away

text: The intern you kept found a way to print invoices double-sided. Savings: two reams a week.
Marketing shows a free ad: staff filmed themselves drinking tea from our kettles. Ten thousand views.
Your line “we don't leave anyone behind” made the local paper. Your mum sends the clipping and three hearts.
The reporter who wrote “A Month to Live” wants an interview: “Looks like I was wrong. How did you do it?”
right: Have her talk to the team

text: The watchman brings tea: “You'd have left first today if it weren't for my tea.” He's right, you finished early.
At home they ask how work is going. For the first time, you want to say not “holding on” but “I think it's working.”
Sales invite you to a little party for the deal: a cake reading “We're Boiling!” It's a bit burnt in places.
The courier who once delivered boxes of unpaid bills now brings an order for a hundred kettles. He recognises you and grins.
right: Check it and send him off

text: The chief engineer fixed the “don't touch” machine. Turns out it just needed touching the right way.
For the first time in six months the shareholders end a call on time and say “carry on.” Nothing more.
Your neighbour asks you to watch her son for half an hour while she's at the clinic. Your creditor call is in forty minutes.
left: Bring the kid to the call

text: Morning: the washing machine flooded the bathroom. The repairman will come “between nine and six.” Board meeting at nine.
left: Ask a neighbour to let him in
right: Run the board call from home

text: The school parents' chat demands an “Autumn Hedgehog” craft by tomorrow. Your last three evenings went into the payment calendar.
The dog ate the printed rescue plan. Only the “Risks” section survived. Apparently it isn't tasty.
Your building's lift is stuck between floors with you inside. No signal. Talks with your biggest supplier in 20 minutes.
Mum calls at 7:30 to check you're dressed warmly. She also asks how “your crisis” is doing. Your crisis is fine.
The school calls: your child got into a scuffle over the last pastry. Someone needs to come in. You're mid-negotiation over debt.
A courier is at your home with a parcel, but you're at the office: “Leave it at the door?” It's a competitor's kettle you ordered to study.
The upstairs neighbours started renovating, drilling exactly when you're working from home on the bank plan.
Your child calls at lunch: “We have to ask our parents what they do for work. What are you?” Deeper than it sounds.
An old friend is in town for one day and invites you to lunch. It clashes with a logistics meeting already postponed twice.
You promised to cook dinner but you're an hour late. Hungry faces and doubt about your promises await.
Your child wants the laptop for homework. The debt spreadsheet is open. Your child is already asking what “overdue” means.
right: Close it all and hand it over

text: The cat chewed through the charger cable just as the laptop hit 3%. The shareholder report isn't saved.
A neighbour on your staircase recognises you: “You're from Luchik? My son works on your floor. Says things got better.”
You've finally run a bath. The phone on the edge flashes: “CFO: urgent.” The water is the perfect temperature.
left: Call back in half an hour

text: Your country neighbour sends a photo: “Everything's dried up except the courgettes. Like you, they're hanging on.”
Your hairdresser has rescheduled you three times, at your request. “Maybe we could at least trim the crisis?”
At school your child drew “my parent's factory” — a storm cloud on top and a sun peeking from the side. The teacher sends a photo.
right: Share it in the team chat

text: Your car won't start, and a taxi to the plant costs a lunch for three. You could take the staff bus with the workers.
At home you're asked if you'd like a seaside trip “when all this is over.” It'll never be over, but you'd love the sea.
The 24-hour shop by your house sells our kettles. At the old price, with a tag that's outlived three directors.
The reception printer stamps the word “DEBT” on top of every page. The sysadmin swears it's not a template, it's “personality.”
Someone hung an “Emergency Room” sign on your office door. Next to it is a doodle of a kettle with a red cross.
right: Ask for it to come down

text: The meeting-room clock has run 17 minutes slow since the last director. Everyone shows up on “meeting-room time.”
The cooler's empty and the water contract was cancelled to save money. Staff carry water in kettles from the shop floor.
A pigeon flew through a broken window and settled on the packing line. The line stopped. The pigeon feels like management.
On a video call the CFO forgot to turn off a filter and presented the debt figures for half an hour as a potato. Everyone listened closely.
right: Let him finish as a potato

text: In the old director's cabinet: forty boxes of chocolates “for partners.” They expire in a week.
The company chatbot glitched and wished every employee a happy birthday at once. Accounting is already bringing a cake.
A fire drill goes off mid-negotiation with the bank. The banker asks if it's a figure of speech.
The ficus nobody sold suddenly bloomed. Staff take it as a sign. The chief accountant thinks it means water it less.
right: Move it to the shop floor

text: The plant's “Days Without Incident” board has said 0 for two weeks. No incidents. The board is just broken.
Security reports an ex-employee tried to get in last night: “I left my mug here five years ago.” The mug was found.
left: Return it with a cup of tea

text: Your office bulb burned out, and you've worked an hour by monitor light. It looks like a crisis room from a movie.
The vending machine ate your last coins and dispensed not a snack bar but a nut. A metal one, probably from the shop floor.
left: Take the nut to the engineers

text: At 8 p.m. marketing sends an idea: a kettle that sings the company anthem when it boils. He's already composed the tune.
The secretary asks what to do with 300 of the old director's business cards. Heavy, quality card stock.
Your office chair costs as much as a foreman's monthly wage. You could sell it and buy a regular one.
The robot vacuum left by the old director rolls out every evening and bumps into the accounting door.
An investor is ready to put in money but wants a board seat and the right to “influence the canteen menu.” He says it's a matter of principle.
The bank wants a daily cash report by 9 a.m. Money is moving, luckily, but the report will eat your mornings.
right: Do it yourself for a week

text: At 7:50 the owner sends you an article: “Ten Signs Your Crisis Manager Is Failing.” No comment.
The owner wants to sell the plant and keep only the brand. “Let others make the kettles.” Half the staff work at the plant.
A venture fund offers money if the company becomes “tech.” Your tech is a smart lamp that's sometimes smart.
The bank manager visits the plant to “see the collateral.” The collateral is the packing line, which just broke down.
The shareholders start arguing with each other mid-meeting. You must pick a side or stay neutral.
The investor wants “one number that explains everything.” You have nine such numbers. He's waiting.
The owner suggests a 20% pay cut for everyone except top managers, “so they don't run off.”
The bank's analyst spots a typo in your plan: “growth 30%” instead of “3%.” He liked it.
The owner calls at 9 p.m. from his holiday: “I was on the beach and had a thought...” Waves, gulls and a new strategy.
The investor invites you to dinner “to talk informally.” Informally means you pay for his oysters while he thinks.
At 7:55 p.m. the bank sends a new contract draft. One clause changed, and it changes everything. The lawyer's already home.
The shareholders want a video report “like big companies do”: charts and music, “upbeat but with a hint of worry.”
The founder who sold the company three years ago texts: “If you need advice, call me. I know where all the skeletons are.”
The morning after dinner, the investor sends a “short term sheet” of eleven pages. Condition one: “transparency.”
right: Hand it all to the lawyer

text: The bank will restructure if you personally guarantee the loan. Personally means your flat is on the line too.
You're drafting three scenarios for shareholders: bad, very bad and “let's not.” The last one is the easiest to write.
The engineer proposes a cheap no-frills kettle: no lights, no tune, it just boils. Working name: “Just a Kettle.”
Marketing wants to rebrand the smart lamp as a “mood lamp.” It still sometimes won't switch on, but now that's a “mood.”
A young engineer built a toaster prototype that burns “Good morning” onto bread. Works every other time, but it's funny.
left: Give him a month to refine it
right: Shelve it: no time for toys

text: Sales wants to sell kettles to offices on a “kettle subscription” with servicing. Odd, but they already have two clients.
A nearby plant wants you to make vacuum cleaner parts for them. Your floor would be busier, but the line needs retooling.
A freelance designer offers to refresh the kettle's look for free, in exchange for showing it in her portfolio.
An analyst finds your most profitable item: spare lids for old kettles, bought by people who broke theirs.
The shareholders are fired up about launching a “smart fridge.” There's no money for a fridge, or even for research.
Support proposes repairing old kettles for a small fee instead of selling new ones. Customers love it. Sales doesn't.
The engineer sends a photo: “Just a Kettle” boiled its first water. Caption: “It just boils. It's beautiful.”
An evening idea: a café at the plant, everything brewed on our kettles. It's either genius or fatigue.
Marketing wants a kettle in the local football team's colours. The whole city loves them, except their scoreline.
The young engineer stays late working on the message toaster. All he asks is to leave the workshop lights on.
right: Ask him to leave on time

text: A restaurant chain wants two hundred industrial kettles. You don't make those, but the engineer says “we'll build them.”
The lawyer warns that someone already registered “Just a Kettle.” That someone is the previous director's former deputy.
left: Come up with a new name

text: The focus group loves the new kettle, but all five want it to “also talk.” The engineer clutches his head.
The team voted on a name for the new kettle. “Kettle of Hope” leads; second place is “Boil Already.”
The CFO suggests nudging next month's revenue into this month “just a little” so the bank report looks better.
A new plastics supplier offers a discount plus a “personal bonus, just for you” for a long contract. The discount's fine. The bonus isn't.
left: Take the discount, not the bonus

text: HR suggests not renewing a contract for an employee about to go on maternity leave: “It saves money.” You don't like it at all.
QC spots a minor flaw in the new batch: a scratch on the base. Customers won't see it. Shipping is today.
An employee admits he sent a client the wrong price. It's in the client's favour, and the client is already delighted.
You've accidentally been forwarded a rival's internal deck with their prices for the next year. Open it?
Sales want ads saying “the most reliable kettle in the country.” No proof, but it sounds great.
The chief accountant says you could “overlook” an old fine nobody remembers. Small amount, big principle.
The intern finds a mistake in your own bank plan. It's not in your favour. The bank meets at nine tomorrow.
right: Fix it, ask for a delay

text: Logistics proposes overloading the trucks: “Everyone does it, a fine's cheaper than an extra trip.”
A journalist offers to “not write about the recall” if you buy an ad in his outlet. The ad is cheap.
The shop chief asks you not to tell upstairs he missed two days for family reasons. He made up the work at night.
The owner asks you to hire his nephew “in any role.” The nephew wants to start as deputy director.
The box supplier sent new boxes with your logo upside down. Reprinting takes a week. Shipping is today.
The customs broker says the heating elements are stuck because the papers describe them as “warm thingies.”
right: Wait for them to sort it

text: A truck driver calls from a ditch: he's fine, everything's intact, but the truck's sideways in a field. The kettles, he says, are “calm.”
left: Send help and a tow truck
right: Tell him to wait for insurance

text: The button supplier admits he's near bankruptcy himself and asks for anything upfront. Without his buttons, kettles won't switch on.
The keeper wants to rearrange the warehouse so bestsellers sit by the gate. Two days' work and one sore back.
left: Do it over the weekend, paid

text: Logistics finds half the trucks return empty. You could haul others' freight back, but it'd take another dispatcher.
The steel supplier offers a new grade 10% cheaper. The engineer says it “rusts if you look at it.”
9 p.m. The truck expected this morning arrives. The loaders have gone home. The driver wants to unload and go.
The dispatcher asks to be paid for night shifts he covered while there was no replacement. No money this month.
The glass supplier is in town for a day and wants a plant tour. Then dinner, but tonight's your family evening.
The stocktake shows 400 extra lids and 400 missing kettles. The kettles and lids clearly fell out.
Logistics proposes sharing delivery with a nearby clothing factory. Kettles would ride alongside pyjamas.
The smart lamp app updated overnight, and now every customer's lamp blinks in Morse code. Decoded, it says “help.”
A developer admits he pushed the lamp update at night “so there'd be less work in the morning.” There's now three times more.
Company email's been down since morning. Staff are passing notes and voice messages. The chief accountant sends reports as photos.
The sysadmin proposes switching from paid software to free alternatives. Huge savings, but everyone has to relearn things.
The shop's online till prints receipts for exactly zero. Customers are thrilled. Accounting isn't.
left: Close the till till it's fixed

text: Your laptop camera dies right before the investor call. You could borrow the intern's, which has an “I Love Kittens” sticker.
The site's up, but the cart freezes at checkout. People add kettles and leave as if they changed their mind about boiling.
The IT contractor wants extra pay for work he “almost finished.” Almost means 40%. He's quite sure that's almost.
An analyst proposes moving all reports into one system. You have four, and they disagree with each other.
The warehouse scanners stopped reading barcodes. The keeper reads them aloud while a colleague types. Slow, but poetic.
An employee sent everyone the accounting system password “so they'd stop asking.” The password is “12345.”
8:30 p.m. The lamp app server is overloaded: everyone switches their lamps on at once because it's dark.
The on-call developer writes: “Everything's stable, but I'm not sure why.” That's worse than when it's broken.
At 10 p.m. your laptop decides to update for 47 minutes. The bank report is inside; you're outside.
A developer asks for a week to “rewrite it all properly.” This is the third time he's asked.
The sysadmin ran a test shutdown to check the backup. The backup has been checked: it doesn't work.
The company post has 300 comments. Half say “bring back the old design,” the other half ask “there was an old design?”
A customer writes to you directly: “Great kettle, but the manual is 40 pages. I'm still on page 12.”
A wave of identical bad reviews hits a review site, all with the same misspelling of “kettle.” Looks like someone's handiwork.
A call centre agent asks permission to tell customers the truth: “Yes, things are tough, but we're trying.” The script says “all great.”
An elderly lady arrives with a 1998 receipt and a kettle that “finally broke.” She wants a warranty repair.
right: Offer a discount on a new one

text: The reviewer who trashed your kettle offers to film “I Was Wrong” if you send a new one. And a toaster.
A café chain complains your kettles are too loud, so customers “can't hear themselves think.” They want a quiet model.
A marketplace demands 15% off or you lose the homepage spot. The homepage is half your sales.
Support wants authority to settle issues up to a set amount without sign-off. Right now every refund goes through you.
A local school asks for a kettle for the staff room: “Ours burned out during a staff meeting.” Sounds like a crisis.
A customer posts a video of your kettle surviving a fall from the second floor. It's going viral. Your lawyer is nervous.
At 11 p.m. a customer writes: “The kettle clicks but won't boil. Or boils but won't click. I'm confused.” Support's asleep.
Last call of the day: a customer rings just to say thanks for a repair. The agent is touched and wants it in training materials.
You're reading reviews before bed. Nine nice ones and one nasty one. Guess which sticks.
Marketing wants a “Oldest Luchik Kettle” contest. Prize: a new kettle. People are already sending photos of antiques.
The CFO comes to work in slippers and hasn't noticed. He's gone three weeks without a day off.
left: Send him home for two days

text: The chief accountant says she can't count debts anymore: “I dream in numbers. Last night I dreamed a ledger entry.”
Your deputy admits he got an offer from a rival. He likes it here, but there it's stable.
The shift foreman asks to move the briefing: his son starts first grade today. Without him the briefing falls apart.
You notice nobody laughs in the office anymore. Not even at the ficus. People seem tired of the word “crisis.”
left: Ban the word for a week

text: An employee is crying in the meeting room after a call from an angry supplier. Your meeting there starts in five minutes.
The logistics head has stayed till late three times this week. He says it's “calmer this way.” He doesn't look calm.
HR proposes an extra day off instead of bonuses. No money needed, and people like it.
Your best salesman asks to be moved to the warehouse: “I'm tired of smiling into the phone.” Sales will dip without him.
The shop chief snaps at workers over nothing. That never used to happen.
At 10:30 p.m. the work chat starts debating tomorrow's task. Six people are typing, all with kids and dogs.
right: Jump in and wrap it up

text: The sysadmin hasn't had a holiday in two years because “everything breaks without me.” Probably true.
Your deputy writes: “Sorry, got nothing done today. My head's not working.” First honest message in a month.
right: Ask for at least a plan

text: The guard says on night shift there's no one to talk to, and the radio only picks up news about your company.
right: Move his post near the floor

text: A young accountant asks to work remotely: “I'm faster at home. The office is always urgent about something.”
The intern does the work of two without a word. Everyone has quickly grown used to dumping tasks on him.
Staff ask if they can leave an hour early once a week, since pay can't go up for now.
The lift mirror shows someone sleeping five hours a night. That someone is you, looking like a cash flow statement.
First sit-down breakfast in a week. The phone lies face down, vibrating like a tiny tractor.
A neighbour offers his bike for the commute. 25 minutes instead of 40 in traffic, though you'll arrive soaked by autumn rain.
The coach suggests writing down three good things a day. Today you've got one: the server didn't break.
Your assistant blocked a daily hour labelled “DO NOT TOUCH.” Creditors are already asking for that slot.
After tough talks you'd love a walk around the plant. But the logistics call is in 15 minutes.
The canteen is making your favourite soup today. The lawyer meeting is set right at lunchtime.
left: Push the lawyer half an hour
right: Take the soup to the meeting

text: Your coach offers 20-minute online workouts at lunch. The camera would show your office walls full of debt charts.
The novel on your nightstand, started last month, still has the bookmark on page 14.
Friends invite you to board games on Friday. You haven't won anything lately except instalment negotiations.
Your phone offers to enable Do Not Disturb from 10 p.m. The CFO asked you to stay reachable “just in case.”
At home you're offered a movie. You pick a comedy. Someone puts on a film about a corporate bankruptcy.
Family dinner. Your child asks if there can be no work talk at the table. You were about to explain the springs.
Morning, rain, traffic. You could call and say you'll be in at ten, or spend an hour stressing to make it by nine.
That's your fifth coffee. Your hands are shaking a bit, and you still have talks with the steel supplier.
The shop chief invites you to a Saturday sauna with the foremen: “We'll sort it all out there, like people.” It's a sign of trust.
The owner wants to rename the company “to shed bad karma.” He already has a name: “Luchik 2.0.”
The shareholders want “one good piece of news” every week. Good news shows up about once a month.
right: Explain it doesn't work like that

text: The owner turns up at the plant unannounced. The floor is mid-clean, everyone dusty and holding buckets.
right: Ask him to wait in the office

text: The owner compares you to the last crisis manager: “At least he shouted. You could see he was working.”
At the board meeting a shareholder asks why the budget has a line for “Friday pie.” It costs next to nothing.
The owner wants the shop chief fired for arguing at a meeting. The shop chief was right.
A minor shareholder calls daily to ask “how's it going.” He owns 0.3% of the shares and 100% of the anxiety.
left: Send him a short weekly note

text: At 9:30 p.m. the owner forwards a photo of someone else's office: “This is how it's done.” It has swings.
The shareholders moved the board meeting to Saturday morning. Your Saturday morning was booked for sleep.
The owner publicly praises you for the first profitable month. But the chief accountant put the numbers together, not you.
The owner wants to address staff personally “to inspire them.” Last time, three people quit after his speech.
A shareholder asks to see “Plan B.” There isn't one, because everything went into Plan A.
The owner offers you a stake if you turn the company around in a year. Sounds great, but it means another year without weekends.
The assembly line stopped over a part worth about as much as a bun. Only a supplier in the next region has it.
The technician says he can retune the line for 50% more output, but only with two days of quiet on the floor.
The energy engineer suggests running the tempering oven on the cheaper night tariff. The night shift won't love it.
The paint shop ran out of white. There's only pink. Ship pink kettles or wait a week.
A worker suggests reordering operations so housings don't get carried across the whole floor. He's suggested it to six directors.
The safety officer finds an extension cord on the floor held together with tape and hope.
The engineer wants to boil-test every tenth kettle on the line. It'll slow the line by 5%.
The floor is sweltering; ventilation is at half power. Workers suggest starting the shift two hours earlier.
In the parts store you find a machine still in its packaging, bought five years ago. Nobody ever unboxed it.
The foreman shows you a jig the workers invented that speeds assembly by 20%. It's made from an old stool.
right: Have engineers make a proper one

text: The packing line works, but it tapes boxes so tightly no customer can open them.
The evening shift beat target by 15%. The foreman asks if everyone can go home an hour early.
At 7:40 p.m. the tempering oven overheats. Stop it and lose the batch, or risk it till end of shift.
The technician calls from the floor: “The line's running, but it sounds different.” He trusts his ears over the gauges.
The night shift asks for a coffee machine on the floor, to “stop nodding off over the lids.”
You stay for a night shift for the first time to see how the plant runs. Workers are surprised and a little wary.
A recruiter found a great engineer, but he wants as much as the whole QC team earns.
A candidate asks at interview: “You won't shut down in a month, will you?” The honest answer is “we hope not.”
An engineer who left six months ago wants back: “It's stable there, but boring.” His seat is still free.
A headhunter calls with a role at a big corporation. “You love crises, right? We don't have any.”
HR suggests taking interns from the local college: free now, staff later. But someone has to train them.
A veteran foreman agrees to train interns but asks for “something” extra for mentoring.
A rival is poaching your welders for 20% more. Two are getting ready to leave.
A worker retires after 35 years at the plant. He wants it quiet, no send-off. The floor wants a send-off.
A college intern stays after shift to learn from his mentor. His mum has called twice asking where he is.
right: Call his mum to reassure her

text: A logistics candidate sends a CV at 11 p.m. marked “can start tomorrow.” It's a good CV.
HR proposes a family open day: kids, tea, a tour of the floor.
A former colleague asks for advice: her company is also being “saved,” and she's scared. You know what to tell her.
The tax office asks why the company bought 300 kg of sweets last year. The answer sits in the old director's cabinet.
The fire inspector arrives. You have extinguishers, but one is being used as a doorstop.
The lawyer proposes suing the former director for “mismanagement.” Middling odds, guaranteed lost nerves.
A creditor files a bankruptcy petition “as a reminder.” The lawyer says it's pressure, but real pressure.
The judge asks why the company ignored three letters from a creditor. They turned up in that “Later” box.
Environmental inspectors ask where recalled kettles go. The answer: “the guest dining room.”
The lawyer finds the old steel contract lets you reclaim two years of overpayment. But the supplier has become a friend.
The auditor finds the “Deputy for Strategic Optimism” is real and has worked remotely from a village for three years.
The Optimism Deputy calls: “All these years I've run the newsletter for the plant's retirees. It matters.”
The lawyer writes in the evening: “Good news, we won the case. Bad news, eight more to go.”
right: Plan for the other eight now

text: The tax office meeting is tomorrow morning. Tonight the chief accountant wants to double-check every document.
A rival sues claiming your new kettle “resembles” theirs. The resemblance is that it's also a kettle.
The safety inspector praises the new gloves and asks where the old ones went. They hang on the floor as a “museum.”
Before bed you tally lawsuits, fines and inspections: thirteen. You're about 4% superstitious.
The secretary asks whether to put up a tree in the lobby. Last year they skipped it “to save money.” There's an old artificial one.
left: Decorate it with our own baubles

text: It snowed overnight; trucks can't get into the yard. One janitor, one shovel, snow for everyone.
The chief accountant reminds you December means annual bonuses. None are budgeted, but people remember there used to be.
The team asks about the New Year party. No money for a restaurant. There's the shop floor, fairy lights and a homemade band.
Pre-holiday demand: twice the usual orders. The warehouse can't keep up, deliveries are slipping.
left: Office staff help in the warehouse

text: Suppliers send New Year gifts. The biggest one is from the supplier who yelled the most.
At the shop-floor party, foreman Petrovich smiles for the first time. Last time, they say, was a decade ago.
Someone has to play the winter gift-bringer at the staff kids' party. Everyone's looking at you.
December 31, 6 p.m. The bank sends a document that “must be signed this year.” You're already on your way to the holiday dinner.
You promised yourself no work during the holidays. By day three your hands reach for the laptop “just to check email.”
First workday of the year. Half the staff are late; the other half came early because they missed the place.
In spring the shop roof starts leaking. A repair eats the whole reserve. You could patch it and wait for summer.
Kettle sales drop in summer. Sales propose selling “water coolers” in the heat. They're jugs.
In summer the team asks about holidays. Everyone at once stops the plant. In turns, someone misses the beach.
right: Close the plant for two weeks

text: Exactly a year ago you walked in with the “Everything Is Bad” folder. The secretary leaves a new one: “Everything's Better.” Three pages.
Payday. Only 80% of payroll came in. The treasurer asks: 80% for everyone, or 100% for some?
A factoring company will buy your receivables right now. Cash today, but 12% less.
The chief accountant finds a truck on the books that's sat wheelless for six months. The wheels apparently left on their own.
right: Fix it for our own routes

text: The foremen chipped in and offer the company a loan to cover the young workers' pay. Small sum, huge gesture.
Sales suggest opening pre-orders for “Just a Kettle” a month before launch. Money comes sooner, and so do expectations.
The CFO shows next month's cash gap is exactly one week. Survivable, if everyone agrees to wait.
A regional dealer will buy a big batch, but pays in 90 days. The order would eat all your stock.
You could sublet half the office to a neighbouring firm. Sales would have to share space with accounting.
Sales found a client willing to pay cash today, but only with 25% off.
Accounting proposes auditing a year of travel expenses. They say there's “a couple of payrolls” in there.
Evening: the treasurer says a big client finally paid. You can clear the steel debt or pay the rest of the wages.
10 p.m. You're shuffling payments in the spreadsheet for the fifth time, like a jigsaw. It won't fit, but the picture looks familiar.
An employee asks for an advance: his car broke down and he can't get to the plant without it. Money is tight.
A dealer calls at 8 p.m.: “I'll pay tomorrow if you send another truckload today.” Sounds familiar.
A rumour says a rival will buy the company and shut the floor. It started with a driver who heard “something in the canteen.”
New rumour: the office is moving to the countryside, “fresh air and cows.” It isn't. The cows will be disappointed.
You've started a weekly staff letter about company news. This is number three. Nothing to report except the roof repair.
You've started monthly all-hands meetings. More people than chairs turned up. Someone brought a stool from home.
At the meeting a worker asks: “Why should we trust you?” The room falls silent.
Someone posted a scan of your bank plan in the general chat. Everyone's discussing the “optimisation” slide.
A staff representative asks for regular meetings to discuss decisions in advance. It'll take time but ease tension.
The evening chat claims you're job hunting. You were hunting for a new dish sponge. In your browser history. On the work laptop.
An anonymous letter: “You're a good person, but one of your deputies is deceiving you.” No name.
The shift foreman says people stopped discussing rumours and started discussing the plan. A first in his memory.
Next to an official memo, someone pinned a note: “Hang in there!” Twenty signatures already.
A sales rep admits telling clients the company is “on the brink” so they'd pay faster. It works, but hurts the brand.
Evening crisis memes in the team chat. One shows you with a fire extinguisher: “Puts out every fire except their inbox.”
11:50 p.m. Security calls: the plant alarm went off. The cameras show only a cat that seems to have lived on the floor for ages.
right: Ask security to do a round

text: The watchman reports a burst pipe on the floor. Ankle-deep water, and shipping in the morning.
right: Call the plumbers, go at dawn

text: In the evening a substation fault cuts power to the plant. The night shift sits in the dark with torches.
The night shift sends a photo: they're playing dominoes by torchlight on a crate of kettles. Power is due in an hour.
right: Ask them to tidy up meanwhile

text: 1:15 a.m. An alert: 400 orders in 10 minutes. Either a bot attack or you were on TV.
Overnight a truck gets stuck on a mountain pass in snow. The driver asks whether to wait for morning or risk it.
The warehouse alarm is keeping the neighbours awake. A mouse set it off. Angry emails are flowing.
The sysadmin asks permission to reboot everything at 2 a.m. “Like turning it off and on, just bigger.”
A late-night message from a customer: “Thanks for the kettle, we're watching the sunrise with it at the cottage.” Photo attached.
A forklift breaks down overnight. The night shift offers to carry boxes by hand to finish by morning.
The CFO writes at night: “I found the forecast error!” Five minutes later: “No, I didn't.”
The office fire alarm goes off at night. Cause: someone left toast in the prototype toaster. The toast reads “Good morning.”
A hotel chain wants your kettles in every room, on condition each carries the hotel's logo.
A distributor abroad wants samples. Shipping them costs a month's ad budget.
A café chain pays on time but asks for a new discount every month. Each one “the last.”
The district schools department wants kettles for every school. The tender needs 90 pages of paperwork.
A corporate client ordered 50 kettles engraved “Employee of the Year.” The engraver wrote “Employe of the Year.”
A dealer from a neighbouring city wants regional exclusivity. In return he promises to double sales.
A client wants a presentation at their office tomorrow at 8 a.m. Their office is three hours away.
A retail partner proposes a joint deal: free toaster with every kettle. The toasters are yours, the profit is shared.
A client sends a 12-page complaint in the evening. At the end: “But your account manager is lovely.”
A sales rep returns from a trade show delighted: “Twenty business cards!” Nineteen are from other salespeople.
A hotel sends a photo: your kettle in the presidential suite looks pricier than the vase next to it.
You propose stand-up meetings to keep them short. The CFO brings a tall bar stool.
Nine people come to a meeting with nothing on the agenda for them. They're there to “stay in the loop.”
Every department sends you a daily report. You read them until lunch. You don't remember lunch.
Your deputy proposes a “one page” rule for all documents. The lawyer is horrified.
The meeting about why meetings run long is now in its second hour.
Managers bring you even paper clip orders to sign. Nobody decides anything without your signature.
A department head starts every task with “under the last director we did it like this.”
You've been cc'd on 600 emails this week. Eight actually concern you.
The evening meeting was called to discuss the morning one, which was called to prepare for the evening one.
Your deputy proposes one meeting-free day a week. Shareholders won't get it; staff will.
Tomorrow's calendar has 11 meetings. Not even five minutes between them for a bathroom break.
Your assistant asks if you need the report three people compile every evening. You've never opened it.
Your deputy made a decision without you for the first time: moved a shipment to avoid a night shift. Debatable, but sensible.
At a strategy session, managers draw the company's future on the whiteboard. Everyone draws a kettle.
Your old mentor calls: “Remember: you don't save companies, you save the people in them. Companies follow.”
left: Write it down and pin it up
right: Ask for advice on the bank

text: You're offered a free evening course, “Managing in a Crisis.” You're already living that course.
The CFO brings you a book, “How to Survive a Crisis.” He didn't finish it: “The crisis started first.”
You're invited to speak at a conference: “How Not to Lay Anyone Off.” The talk isn't finished, nor is the crisis.
A crisis manager from another company suggests a monthly lunch to swap notes.
The intern asks how you learned not to panic. You're not sure you have.
You've started noting each evening what went well. Today: dinner on time.
Your mentor offers a weekly call to review your decisions. Another call, but a useful one.
On the way home you listen to a business podcast. The host describes a company much like yours. It closed at the end.
The foreign distributor writes only in English. Your English stops at “kettle” and “thank you.”
right: Battle on with a translator app

text: Your former boss calls: “Heard you're saving kettles. Proud of you.” He rarely praises anyone.
The kindergarten next door asks you to fix their old kettles for free. There are eight, all different.
The district paper wants a feature on the plant for its “Our Local Businesses” column. No scandals, photos of foremen.
The technical college wants a student tour. The floor is mid-renovation and smells of paint.
The plant retirees' club asks to meet in the canteen once a month. They'll bring the tea; you provide the room.
A charity asks for kettles for a shelter. There's no money for charity, but there are scratched seconds.
Residents nearby complain about early-morning loading noise. You could start later, but shipments would slip.
Staff propose a Saturday clean-up: paint the fence, plant trees by the gate. You'd come too.
You're offered a stall at the town fair, serving tea from your kettles. The stall costs money.
At the fair the queue for free tea stretches across the square. Foremen pour, you hand out cups.
After the tour, students write in: three want placements. There's nobody free to teach them.
A neighbour who works in your warehouse knocks in the evening: “I've got a warehouse idea. Got a minute?”
right: Ask him to bring it tomorrow

text: The shelter sends a photo: the kettles in their kitchen, next to the kids' drawing saying “Thank you.” You want to hang it on the floor.
An analyst built a dashboard with 48 charts. All you can tell is that it's colourful.
left: Ask for the three key ones

text: This morning you notice warehouse turnover improved 20%. The keeper says she just stopped hiding boxes.
The CFO wants profit tracked per kettle model. Turns out the red one loses money.
Sales want bonuses tied to revenue. The CFO wants them tied to profit. The chief accountant dislikes both.
An analyst finds 70% of support calls are the same question: how to descale the kettle.
Unit cost fell 7% thanks to switching back to the good old springs. Defects fell even more.
Two departments keep the same spreadsheet independently. Their figures differ by a million.
At 9 p.m. the analyst sends a forecast: at this pace, the company breaks even in five months.
You're staring at the sales chart. The line has finally ticked up, just slightly. You could watch it another hour.
The bank report balances, except one cell shows “#DIV/0!”. That's exactly what the bank will look at first.
left: Track it down and fix it

text: The shareholders want an “employee happiness” metric. HR suggests counting smiles at stand-up.
The wire supplier sends an invoice marked “third reminder, final, honestly.” You never got the first two.
right: Ask for copies of the letters

text: Before supplier talks, the CFO suggests “good cop, bad cop.” You'd be the bad one, naturally.
The steel supplier offers to lock in a price for a year. It's high now but could rise further.
A new plastics supplier is 20% cheaper, but his samples smell like rubber boots.
The plastics supplier who camped in reception now wants to be friends: “You're the first who's been straight with me.” He offers a discount.
A supplier has haggled over every penny for three hours. You've even discussed the delivery cost of paper clips.
Neighbouring plants propose buying electricity together. Cheaper, but schedules must align.
A supplier offers payment terms in exchange for his logo on your boxes.
The button supplier you helped with an advance survived and sent a batch with a gift: heart-shaped buttons.
In the evening a supplier writes that prices go up Monday, “but for you, Tuesday.” Generous by exactly one day.
After talks with the carrier, logistics returns voiceless but with a price 15% lower.
A supplier suggests continuing talks over dinner. You're tired, but dinner could mean a discount.
The glass supplier apologises: a batch arrived cracked. He offers to replace everything plus ten percent extra.
The press team asks to answer social comments without sign-off, “before it becomes a meme.”
A business magazine wants you in its “Top Crisis Managers of the Year” list. Participation costs money.
A video online shows a loader kicking a box of your kettles. The box is yours, the loader isn't, but who'll check?
The press team wants to show customers' kettles being repaired on social media. “The human face of the company.”
A reporter wants a plant tour to write an “honest piece.” Her last honest piece was a hatchet job.
A forum invites you to a panel on “Surviving a Crisis.” Your fellow panellist is that rival.
One article mixed you up with the former director and reported that you'd left.
A piece runs: “How Luchik Boiled Again.” Not a word about you, plenty about the foremen.
The press officer suggests a channel called “A Crisis Manager's Diary.” You'd write every evening.
At 10 p.m. a journalist asks about last year's recall: “Could it happen again?” You're at home in pyjamas.
A video of workers singing at the party went viral. The press team is delighted, the foremen mortified.
right: Take it down for the foremen

text: A firmware update makes the smart kettle send owners “I've boiled!” notifications at 6 a.m., even when nobody switched it on.
The smart lamp app has a 1.8 rating. Top complaint: “The lamp is sulking and won't turn on.”
The sysadmin wants a new UPS for the server room. The old one lasts four minutes, if you're lucky.
A developer proposes open-sourcing the lamp code: “The community will fix it.”
Accounting got an email “from the bank” asking to confirm a password. The chief accountant nearly did, then asked first.
The contractor delivers the new website. It's beautiful, but the “Buy” button is buried at the bottom.
The new site has run a week without a hitch. The sysadmin sleeps at night now. Says he “feels weird.”
right: Ask him to test the backup

text: An evening complaint: the smart kettle joined the neighbours' Wi-Fi and is boiling water for them.
10 p.m. You realise nobody has tested restoring the backup. The sysadmin is on holiday.
The support chatbot now answers customers with quotes from the manual. To “how are you?” it replies “do not immerse in water.”
A developer proposes an on-call rota so nobody gets woken every night. The rota needs one more person.
The new warehouse software works. The keeper still keeps a paper log “just in case.”
QC proposes that any worker can stop the line on spotting a defect. The shop chief fears downtime.
The engineer wants to boil-test the new kettle 10,000 times. A month of testing, and sales are waiting.
A customer who got a recall replacement writes: “The new one's better than the old. Can you recall it again?”
right: Offer a discount on a second

text: QC finds the new supplier's lids are a millimetre too thick. The kettle shuts only with effort.
The engineer proposes publishing quality reports on the website. Honest, but rivals will read them too.
A customer claims your kettle “boils too fast.” He doesn't have time to pick his tea.
Selling to a chain requires a new certificate. The lab is booked two months out; express service costs extra.
The inspector stays late re-checking the last batch. It's perfect, but she can't believe it.
left: Check with her, then send her off

text: A year after the recall, a letter arrives: a customer bought a second kettle “because you didn't lie back then.”
At 8 p.m. the engineer is still comparing springs under a magnifying glass. Forty of them on the desk.
Your child asks for a ride to school: “You haven't taken me in a month.” It'll take forty minutes.
Your kettle at home broke. It's a rival brand, bought a year ago before you joined.
You wake at 4:30 thinking about the steel supplier and can't fall back asleep. Ninety minutes till the alarm.
The plants on your windowsill have dried out. Your neighbour offers “crisis-proof” new ones. They're cacti.
right: Try to revive the old ones

text: Your parents invite you to Sunday lunch. You promised yourself Sunday for the quarterly plan.
The school parents' evening is at 5 p.m. So is your bank meeting.
A friend writes that he's in a work crisis and asks for advice. You know the answer, but you're in one too.
First home-cooked dinner in a month. The phone rings just as the onions start to burn.
Your child needs help with a maths problem about two pipes filling a pool. You spent the day on a debts-and-payments problem.
A neighbour invites you to a birthday on the landing. Cake, tea and one of your kettles. You've just got home.
You started a series three months ago and are stuck on episode two. Tonight is free.
The family wants a weekend away somewhere with no signal. None at all, not even on the hill.
The dog wants a walk at 6:30. You'd planned to answer emails then. The dog had other plans.
The tap at home has been dripping for two days. The plumber can only come today at three.
For the first time, foreman Petrovich drops by your office on his own. No complaints, just “for a cup of tea.”
right: Ask him to come after lunch

text: The warehouse keeper challenges you to lunchtime chess. Says she's played and beaten every director.
A “Thanks This Week” board has appeared on the floor where people thank each other. Your name isn't on it yet.
A new warehouse worker says he joined “because I heard things got decent here.”
The chief accountant says accounting now has a Friday pie tradition. They used to drink only herbal calmers.
The shop chief you used to argue with publicly backs your decision at the meeting.
Repeat survey: trust in management rose from 2.1 to 5.8. A comment: “The new one at least listens.”
Sales came up with a new client approach on their own, without being told. It's unusual.
In the team chat someone writes: “Thanks for not giving up.” It gets 80 hearts in ten minutes.
The guard says staff now leave on time and smiling. “They used to walk out like after an interrogation.”
The night foreman invites you to his milestone birthday: “You're one of us now.” It's on Saturday.
The intern you kept passed probation and brings you cupcakes. They're a bit lopsided; he baked them himself.
left: Eat one in front of him

text: Someone left “DO NOT ERASE” on the meeting-room whiteboard. Underneath is a diagram nobody can explain.
A company selling “courses for crisis managers” calls. They want you as the face of their ads.
Your parking space still has the old director's name plate. The guard says it was “welded on.”
The office lift plays a tune picked by the old director: “Never Give Up.” 24 hours a day.
The cook backs the crisis spirit with new menu names: “Restructuring Cutlet” and “Cash Gap Soup.”
A courier delivers a huge box in your name: a hundred rubber ducks, ordered from the old director's computer a year ago.
A sign appears on the restroom door: “No meetings in here.” Apparently there had been.
The pigeon that once landed on the packing line is back. Now it sits on your office window reading your report.
In the evening you learn all of accounting runs off one socket via six extension cords. The socket is warm.
The rubber ducks have become the company's unofficial mascot. One on every desk. Even the lawyer's.
right: Don't turn it into a brand

text: The coffee machine is back and working, but only dispenses hot water. You're a kettle company. Perfect.
The server-room fan has started humming something like the company anthem. The sysadmin swears he didn't touch it.
For the first time the shareholders ask not “when's the profit” but “what does the team need?” It catches you off guard.
The owner wants to visit the night shift “to understand the people.” The night shift won't be thrilled.
The investor who turned you down six months ago now calls: “We're taking another look.”
The owner wants a banquet for management to mark the first profitable month. The floor isn't invited.
A shareholder wants dividends from the first profit. The CFO wants it invested in machinery.
The owner admits: “I almost sold it all last year. Glad I didn't.”
right: Remind him the job isn't done

text: The owner writes at 10 p.m.: “Don't reply now, get some rest.” First message like that all year.
The board offers to extend your contract a year. You're tired, but things are only just starting to work.
right: Ask for a month's leave first

text: Over dinner the investor asks your secret. You think it over: probably the people. And the tea.
The minor shareholder who called daily now calls weekly. He says “the anxiety's gone.”
right: Invite him to tour the plant

text: The owner wants to give you a bonus. You know the chief accountant and foremen did the most.
right: Take it, buy them a cake

text: Your biggest client cancels an order this morning: “We're reviewing purchasing.” Half the monthly target gone in one email.
A rival slashed prices 30%. Sales are panicking and want to match it by lunch.
A client who owes you a large sum declares bankruptcy. The lawyer says you'll recover “roughly nothing.”
right: Write it off and move on

text: The chief engineer is leaving for a rival in two weeks. He's the only one who knows the old line.
right: Ask him to train a successor

text: Emergency midday meeting: warehouse flooded, site lagging, supplier late. Everyone looks to you for where to start.
The bank unexpectedly froze the account “for review.” Payday is in two days.
left: Go to the bank in person

text: Staff heard about the frozen account and worry about pay. The corridor is quiet and tense.
right: Fix it first, tell them later

text: The lid supplier's warehouse burned down. Nobody was hurt, but there'll be no lids for a month.
A client received a mixed-up shipment: kettles in the toaster boxes. He doesn't much mind, but rules are rules.
right: Offer a discount to keep them

text: Evening meeting: the account is unfrozen, but only 80%. The rest after another review.
On his way out, the chief engineer stays late writing a manual for the old line. Forty pages, illustrated.
The bankrupt ex-client texts in the evening: “Sorry. When I'm back on my feet, I'll come back to you.”
You get in at 7:30 before anyone else. Silence, coffee, no calls. Work, or just sit for a bit?
Before a tough creditor call, your coach's advice: breathe in for four, out for six. The creditor's already on the line.
You haven't had a holiday in eighteen months. Your assistant found a week when nothing's on fire. For now.
Your deputy says: “Go on holiday, I've got it.” He's never been in charge for more than a day.
You have a whole lunch hour. A café by the river, or a meeting over a sandwich?
Your fitness band says your resting heart rate matches a marathoner at the finish line. You're sitting in a meeting.
Day one of your holiday. Your phone buzzes: “Nothing urgent, just keeping you posted.” Five of those already.
You're at the sea. For the first time in eighteen months you're thinking not about debt, but which ice cream to get.
You're back from holiday. Your deputy handled everything; nothing broke. Slightly hurtful, mostly wonderful.
You've taken to walking half an hour after work. Today it's raining and chores await.
HR set up morning stretches for the office. Four people came. You could be the fifth.
Your office has no window, and it took three months to notice it's a former storeroom.
left: Move to one with a window

text: At 7 p.m. a rep needs a discount approved for a client who wants an answer “right now or I'm gone.”
The chief accountant leaves a note on her way out: “It all balanced. First time ever. Don't touch anything till morning.”
The cleaner finds you asleep at your desk at 9 p.m. and asks if she should call a taxi.
At 8 p.m. logistics reports a truck with a key order stopped for inspection. The driver's calm; the logistics head isn't.
The CFO invites you to dinner to go over the quarter “informally.” You're both hungry and grumpy.
An evening text from an unknown number: “This is foreman Petrovich's son. Dad says you're a good one. Thank you.”
