Accounting offers to stay late clearing the archive to free up a room. Pizza's on you.
On the way home the taxi driver tells you how his firm went bust ten years ago. He says he's happy now.
The watchman offers to teach you backgammon “for the nerves.” Says the old director never learned.
The warehouse evening shift finished the stocktake: it all matches, even the minus seven kettles. Found behind a cabinet.
At home you put on one of your own kettles and notice for the first time how quiet it is. The engineer's suffering paid off.
A late video call with regional dealers. One joined from his car, one from a sauna, one with a baby on his lap.
The chief accountant's daughter drew you a card: “Thank you for Mum being home by six.” Her mum hands it over, embarrassed.
left: Pin it up in the office

text: You stayed late, and the last staff bus leaves in 5 minutes. The report isn't finished.
The office manager proposes dropping branded paper calendars next year. Nobody flips past February anyway.
right: Print a few for the foremen

text: The keeper needs new shelving; the old ones sag under the kettles. It's either money or risk.
The engineer wants to visit a trade fair to see new materials. He'll pay the ticket; the days come out of work time.
right: Ask him to go at the weekend

text: A rep asks to work from home on Fridays: clients only phone anyway.
The security firm is raising prices. The watchman says he can manage alone with a radio and tea.
Accounting proposes going paperless. The chief accountant is in favour but asks for a month to adjust.
The head of sales wants to send top reps to a paid training. They'd be out three days.
A neighbour in the industrial park offers to swap your spare pallets for his spare boxes. Your warehouse is becoming a bazaar.
Staff ask to move the smoking area away from the entrance so clients won't see. The new spot is by the bins.
Marketing wants to shoot an ad with the foremen instead of actors. They agree, as long as they don't have to smile.
The lid supplier rebuilt after the fire and shipped to you first. “You helped me, I remember.”
The plant's back yard is piled with old metal. A scrap dealer will haul it and pay. Veterans call it “history.”
left: Sell it, keep a few relics

text: The insurer will pay out for the flooded warehouse but wants forty documents. Twenty you've never heard of.
A building firm wants to rent your idle forklift for a month. It's idle because it's half-broken.
The chief accountant lists everyone who owes the company. Thirty clients, from pennies to fortunes.
A small shop has owed you for ages. The owner says honestly: “I can't pay, but I can give you a display case.”
The CFO finds you've overpaid for phone and internet: tariffs unchanged in five years. A new plan is half the price.
The showroom holds ten years of display models. They could be sold to “vintage appliance” collectors.
The evening auction of old kettles draws a bigger crowd than expected. The oldest sells for the price of three new ones.
The chief accountant says a third of old receivables came in this month. “Nobody's called them like that. Politely, but daily.”
You tally how much you saved without layoffs. It's more than the CFO's plan with layoffs would have saved.
The energy engineer proposes motion sensors for corridor lights. For a few weeks everyone will be waving in the dark.
Sales and the warehouse haven't spoken in a week. Sales promises what's not in stock; the warehouse stopped answering.
The packaging designer is on version nine: “The blue isn't the right blue.” The printer is waiting.
Your longest-serving worker refuses the new software: “Managed forty years without it.” His work is excellent.
A call centre staffer is telling everyone she saw you “in tears” in your car. You were sneezing.
The office joker posted a “crisis timetable for the week” in the lift. It's funny, but shareholders are in the building today.
Two foremen are feuding over whose shift left a dirty machine. Day three of the feud.
A new sales rep closed a deal the old-timers had given up on. The old-timers are sulking.
Sales and the warehouse finally made peace and held a joint tea. You weren't invited, and that's wonderful.
The company's chief sceptic catches you after the meeting: “Fine, I admit it. Not as bad as I thought.”
The designer admits losing sleep over the wrong blue. The new mock-up is perfect, but late.
right: Praise him, ask for earlier drafts

text: One of your best people is always 20 minutes late but leaves an hour after everyone else.
right: Ask him to be on time

text: A customer wants a refund because “the water tastes like water.” He expected more.
A customer brings a kettle that “fell by itself.” From the third floor. Under warranty.
Support wants to answer customers in plain human language, signed with the agent's name. It's slower.
A customer writes that the kettle helped her make up with her neighbour, who came over for tea. She thanks “everyone who made it.”
left: Pin the letter on the floor

text: The service centre in another city has closed. Customers there have nowhere to take kettles for repair.
An office client wants a kettle that “won't let staff take tea breaks over 10 minutes.” The engineer is appalled.
A customer asks to buy a lid from a recalled kettle “as a keepsake.” It was his favourite lid.
An agent accidentally signed off to a customer with “Kisses.” The customer replied “You too.” No complaint.
A customer rings in the evening and spends half an hour describing jam made on your hotplate. You don't make hotplates.
For the first time a company post has more praise than complaints. The press officer sends a screenshot with five exclamation marks.
A customer sends a photo: a hamster lives in his kettle. The kettle's unplugged; the hamster's content. He wants advice.
In the morning you catch yourself thinking: what if you're just buying time, and the company can't be saved?
You notice you've started saying “we” instead of “they” about the company. Looks like you're here for the long haul.
Your call on the new carrier backfired: two deliveries late. Everyone's waiting to see if you'll admit it.
After lunch you realise you've read the same email four times without understanding a word.
A fellow fixer boasts he got his company into profit in six months. By cutting half the staff.
Close the loss-making brand store or give it three more months? Two clerks with fifteen years' service work there.
right: Close it, move them to service

text: In the evening it feels like everything you do is a drop in the ocean. Then a message: “Record shipment today.”
At home the mirror shows someone who aged two years in one, but smiles more than a year ago.
Your coach suggests writing a letter to yourself on day one here. You don't know where to start.
You can't sleep, replaying the day's decisions. One was definitely wrong; the rest, who knows.
left: Write it down and let go

text: The first spare money has appeared. Buy a new machine, or give the floor a 5% raise?
The new machine has arrived but won't fit through the shop gate, built last century for last century's machines.
right: Assemble it inside piece by piece

text: The new machine needs training. The maker offers a one-week course. Sending everyone would stop the line.
right: Train one, who teaches the rest

text: The energy engineer proposes solar panels on the warehouse roof. Payback in six years, if the sun cooperates.
A contractor proposes automating packing. Four packers would no longer be needed there.
The packers heard about automation and ask what happens to them. You promised no layoffs.
The engineer wants a “quiet room” for breaks on the floor. There's an old storeroom for it.
In the evening the new machine produces its first housings. Smoother than anything made here in ten years.
right: Send a photo to the owner

text: The worker who mastered the new machine first asks for a grade promotion. Everyone's watching.
The CFO asks what's next: roof repair, another machine, or a winter reserve. Decide by morning.
The old “don't touch” machine is being retired. The foremen want it displayed by the gate as a monument.
The chief accountant prepares the year's results. For the first time, the profit line isn't negative. Small, but ours.
HR tallies the year: not a single layoff, and staff turnover halved. Even she's surprised.
left: Put it in the shareholder report

text: The steel supplier who called on day one invites you to his firm's anniversary: “We wouldn't be here without you either.”
At the year-end meeting, Petrovich speaks: “I didn't believe. Now I do. Just don't leave.”
right: Say the team can manage without you

text: The shareholders offer to keep you on as a regular director, not a crisis one. Boring work, they say.
The reporter who wrote “A Month to Live” sends a new headline for approval: “The Year That Was Lived.”
The year-end party is on the shop floor again, now with a real stage the foremen built. You're asked to give a toast.
right: Hand the mic to the foremen

text: You find the original “Everything Is Bad” folder. It's thinner now: you took out half the problems and solved them.
You get home at six. Your family looks at the clock, then at you. Dinner isn't even started.
The watchman gives you a key to the gate: “You're one of us now, keep it.” The most precious award of the year.
The CFO wants an 8% price rise: costs went up. Sales fear clients will walk.
Petty cash is short by about three lunches. The log says “taken for needs.” Whose needs, unstated.
The company card shows a purchase: “inflatable pool.” The employee says it was “for testing kettle buoyancy.”
You ask every department to justify its budget from zero. Managers look at you as if you'd asked for a thesis.
left: Give a template and a week

text: Facilities finds a five-year stash of pens in the sales cupboard. Sales say pens “keep disappearing.”
You propose a rule: train travel for trips under six hours. The sales reps sigh.
Your bank charges a fee per payment. The CFO found one with no fees, but switching takes a month.
The firm renting half your office is late with rent. “You know how it is,” they say. You do.
Managers send in their budgets in the evening. All cut 10%, except IT, which asked for 30% more.
The CFO writes: “The tax refund came in. Not much, but unexpected.” He adds three exclamation marks.
Accounting finds you've paid security for five years on a building sold six years ago.
The warehouse proposes reusable crates for store deliveries. Costly now, cheap in a year.
Logistics proposes shipping kettles to stores by rail. Cheaper, but four days slower.
Your courier firm mixed up addresses and delivered a hundred kettles to a dental clinic. The clinic is delighted.
Two drivers retired and nobody's replacing them. Trucks are idle. The logistics head offers to drive himself.
The engineer designed a box using a third less cardboard. But it only opens with instructions.
Stores don't return pallets. This year you lost a small car's worth of them.
The warehouse landlord offers a smaller unit on the same street. A third cheaper, but a week to move.
Logistics wants route-planning software. Right now a foreman plans routes with a map and coloured pencils. Perfectly.
Moving night. Half the boxes are at the new warehouse, half at the old one, and the movers are spent.
A driver calls from the highway: delivery done, and the client gave him a crate of apples. Can he keep it?
Logistics suggests night runs: empty roads, faster delivery. Drivers aren't keen.
There aren't enough laptops: three newcomers share one in shifts. You could buy new ones, but that kills the reserve.
The intern wrote a little script that compiles the morning report automatically. It used to take three people an hour.
right: Test it for a month first

text: The old accounting system only runs on a 2007 PC. It roars like a jet and heats like an iron.
Staff say video calls are wearing them out. They propose Friday calls with cameras off.
The master payments spreadsheet was accidentally deleted. There's a backup, but it's a week old.
Staff use personal phones for work calls. They ask for compensation.
The sysadmin proposes three-word passwords instead of “12345.” The assistant asks if she can write hers on a sticky note.
The server runs faster at night than in the day. The sysadmin found out accounting watches cat videos at lunch.
The accounting software update must go in tonight or it'll stop working tomorrow.
Before his holiday, a developer leaves a note: “If anything breaks, don't touch it till I'm back.”
A hidden page on the site offers “90% off for insiders.” A previous marketer made it and forgot.
The company is nominated for a regional “Comeback of the Year” award. The ceremony falls on your holiday.
A student paper wants an interview on “how to become a crisis manager.” You're not quite sure how you did.
A photo of “your” kettle melted on a stove is going around. It's someone else's kettle and stove.
Regional TV invites you to a live debate with a rival: “Who Makes the Best Kettles?”
A well-known vlogger livestreams unboxing your kettle and can't open the box on air.
A forum claims your plant is “held together with duct tape.” Foreman Petrovich wants to reply personally.
The company wins “Comeback of the Year.” On stage you're asked to say a few words.
After the debate the rival shakes your hand: “It'd be boring without you.” He suggests talking about shared suppliers.
The press officer wants to compile a book, “Luchik's Year,” from staff stories. A lot of work for her.
The journalist who asked whether you could work a kettle wants an interview. A kettle sits on your desk.
The logistics head is taking six months' parental leave. Someone must cover, and there's no budget for a hire.
The warehouse keeper is getting married and has invited the whole warehouse. Same day as a big shipment.
An accountant wants to move to sales: “I love numbers, but I love people more.” Accounting will struggle without her.
right: Ask her to wait a quarter

text: An employee brought her daughter in: the nursery is closed. The girl is drawing on the meeting whiteboard.
right: Suggest she take the day off

text: A foreman turns 60. The floor wants to give him a fishing rod, but chipping in is hard right now.
left: Top it up from the fund

text: An employee asks for a day off to see his son off to university in another city. It's the day of an important inspection.
An employee admits he's taken an evening side job because his pay isn't enough. He's tired and making mistakes.
A new warehouse worker stays late daily, afraid of falling behind. He's slow but accurate.
A foreman texts that his wife is unwell and he needs a few days. Nobody can cover his shift.
left: Let him go, cover it yourself
right: Let him go, ask the next shift

text: An employee returns from parental leave. Her job now runs on a system she doesn't know. She's afraid she won't cope.
left: Give her a month to adapt

text: The owner suggests opening a second plant “since things are going well.” The first one has only just stopped coughing.
The shareholders want a five-year strategy. You've been living in five-week plans.
The owner wants to star in a kettle commercial himself. He's a bit camera-shy.
A new shareholder bought a small stake and demands to see “everything, warehouse to canteen.” Today.
The owner asks who on the team could run things if you left. The question stumps you.
The owner sends a seven-minute voice message in the evening. The first six are about weather and fishing.
After the board meeting, shareholders stay for tea on the floor. One asks to be taught how to assemble a kettle.
The owner asks you to come to an industry dinner and “introduce him to everyone.” You know everyone; he knows nobody.
Your assistant asks to run your calendar more strictly: five meetings a day, max.
The engineer wants to name the new kettle model after foreman Petrovich. Petrovich objects.
left: Name it if he comes round

text: At 8 p.m. marketing sends 14 holiday card options and asks you to pick “by gut, in a minute.”
right: Ask for the top three tomorrow

text: A batch of boxes arrives, each labelled “Fragile: glass kettles.” Your kettles aren't glass.
right: Leave them, they'll be handled gently

text: A bank text at 9:30 p.m.: “Your application is approved.” You can't recall which one. There were four.
The brand-store cashier counts the evening takings and finds an extra thousand. A customer must have overpaid.
The CFO sends the quarterly forecast with a note: “If it all goes wrong, see the ‘Plan C’ tab.” There's no such tab.
The watchman finds a forgotten pot of soup in the canteen and asks if he can eat it “so it doesn't go to waste.”
Someone in the chat asks if they can come in pyjamas on Friday “to boost morale.” A vote is under way.
A café owner writes in the evening: “Your kettle is our star; guests want tea only from that one.”
The guard suggests playing radio for the night shift. Music, he says, speeds up work 10%.
Stuck in traffic on the way home, you call an old friend. He's so happy he talks for an hour.
The night shift asks for Friday pie too, like accounting. Friday arrives later at night.
Late at night an unexpected order for a thousand toasters comes in. There are nine hundred.
Cooking dinner, you catch yourself humming the company anthem marketing wrote. A worrying sign.
Sales ask you not to call after seven at month-end: “We'll close it all anyway.”
Your cat has learned to switch the kettle on with a paw. Without water, so far. Safety needs addressing.
left: Pitch a lock to the engineer

text: Your sister invites you over for pies on Saturday. You promised to review regional reports that day.
There's a queue at the gate: the turnstile only works on the third try. The guard knows everyone by sight anyway.
The morning meeting starts coffeeless: the machine's out for repair. Everyone looks glum.
Your assistant reports two meetings at the same time today on opposite sides of town.
The chief accountant needs 140 documents signed by lunch. E-signatures would work, but yours isn't set up.
In the morning the floor finds a note from nights: “Line 2 was moody, we talked it round.” No details.
Logistics brings news: a bridge on the route is closed, trucks must detour. Half a day extra.
right: Say nothing, we might make it

text: The shift supervisor asks you to personally congratulate the crew: a year without injuries.
Facilities proposes moving sales next to the warehouse. The move would take a weekend.
A morning email from a schoolboy: “I'm doing a project on your plant. Can I ask five questions?”
right: Hand it to the press team

text: Marketing pitches a slogan: “Luchik: warmth that never cools.” The CFO wants “Luchik: cheap.”
The bank sends a happy-anniversary message. A year ago it threatened to seize collateral.
The intern is late because he helped an elderly woman carry her bags to the bus stop. He's been apologising for five minutes.
At 7:15 the head of sales sends a voice note: “Great news, but I'll tell you in person.”
QC wants photos of defects posted on the floor “so everyone knows the enemy.” Foremen find it humiliating.
The canteen is out of forks: people take them home. The cook suggests handing them out against staff passes.
Managers argue over whose department matters most to the rescue. Voices rise.
A major client invites you to lunch and asks for an exclusive price “as an old friend.” You've been friends three weeks.
right: A perk instead of a discount

text: The floor's air conditioning broke on a 30-degree day. The shop chief suggests a shorter shift.
The warehouse keeper asks to hire her niece. The young woman is capable, but family is family.
The CFO suggests leaving the pricey business centre for the plant building. The office would sit by the noisy floor.
Sales bring a client who wants to see the plant. Today it looks like a renovation hurricane just passed through.
The lawyer asks for an hour to explain a new law. The hour becomes three, the law a lecture.
The engineer wants an “Ideas of the Week” board on the floor. Ideas will come, he says, but someone has to read them.
Marketing suggests a livestream from the floor showing kettle assembly. Foremen agree, as long as they don't have to talk.
A delegation from a nearby plant arrives to learn “how you pulled through.” The timing: your lunch break.
The call centre needs new headsets: the old ones crackle, and customers think the agents have colds.
The shop chief asks you not to drop by unannounced: “People get nervous, they think it's an inspection.”
right: Come more often so they get used to it

text: The press team wants a customer newsletter with tea recipes. Accounting has the recipes.
A sales rep asks you to mentor her. Someday she wants to rescue companies too.
The steel supplier proposes co-developing a new housing: his steel, your design, shared sales.
For the first time the site outsold the stores. The retail team is miffed.
Your alarm didn't go off; you wake at 8:40. Meeting at nine, still in pyjamas.
A rival proposes agreeing a regional “minimum price” for kettles. That's illegal and unpleasant.
The inspector requires first-aid training for all staff. It's a full day, which would stop the floor.
The engineer sends a photo: the first “Kettle of Hope” batch is packed. Someone drew a smiley on every box.
A late email: “Your kettle won a design contest.” A contest you didn't enter. The freelance designer did.
Your country neighbour brings a jar of courgette spread: “For not giving up.” The courgettes survived, by the way.
The logistics head drops in from parental leave for half a day “to see how you're doing.”
The chief accountant takes her first holiday in a year. Accounting copes, but keeps calling her “just once.”
Stuck in traffic, you'll be late for a supplier meeting. Call from the car or text at the lights?
At stand-up it turns out two departments are doing the same work without knowing. Both are proud of it.
Overnight someone else's shipment was delivered: two hundred boxes of cat food. The driver's gone.
right: Lend it to a shelter meanwhile

text: The shop chief asks you to speak to the new shift: “Say something, they listen to you.”
An accountant brings a cake: it's a year since wages were last paid late. He's been counting.
Marketing wants to give the first hundred “Kettles of Hope” to staff before sales start. The CFO objects.
right: Sell them at a staff discount

text: The guard complains his gatehouse kettle broke. It's a rival brand. Almost symbolic.
An email from someone the old director fired: “Heard things are good there now. Would you take me back?”
At the floor's morning stretch you're in the front row for the first time. The foremen cheer you on.
Morning: 300 pre-orders for the “Kettle of Hope.” The warehouse asks if it's a glitch.
The CFO invites you to run to work together. He took up running “so the spreadsheets don't drive me mad.”
The engineer wants a trip to the supplier's plant to check the springs in person.
Your assistant reports zero meetings today. That hasn't happened since your first day.
right: Wander the floor for no reason

text: Today the alarm is set for 7:30, not 6:00. Your small victory over the crisis.
At the morning meeting nobody has bad news. Everyone's a little lost about what to discuss.
A courier delivers a parcel from the plastics supplier: a kettle his kids built from offcuts. Note: “To our rescuer.”
right: Give it to the plant museum

text: Foreman Petrovich asks to be trained on the new machine: “I want to understand this electronics in my old age.”
right: Pair him with the young ones

text: A rival “accidentally” emails a job ad for your engineer to your general inbox. The engineer has already seen it.
Before work your child hands you a drawing: “That's your factory and that's you drinking tea.” Everyone's smiling.
Logistics proposes sharing trucks to the next town with the bakery. The truck smells of bread. So will the kettles.
The shareholders send their first email with no questions. Just “Thanks to the team.”
In the evening the CFO admits he'd been sure of failure early on and was job hunting. Not anymore.
The evening warehouse shift held an order-picking race. The winner is the keeper, aged 58.
A text from the intern: “I solved a client's problem on my own today. You'd be proud.” You are.
right: Ask to hear about it tomorrow

text: A surprise at home: your family bought you a pool pass. “So you swim in something other than debt.”
At the pool you think about nothing for the first time in a year. Your phone in the locker missed three calls.
The work chat debates a name for a new product. The most popular pitch is “The Crisis Toaster.”
The shop chief invites you fishing on Sunday: “It's quiet, not a phone in sight.” You've never fished.
You caught nothing on the fishing trip, but the shop chief shared three ideas for the floor. Two are brilliant.
Closing the laptop tonight, you realise there wasn't a single fire today. Not even a small one.
Your neighbour from the warehouse says his son was taken on as a trainee. “I wouldn't have recommended it before.”
right: Promise to keep an eye out

text: A late call with the bank ends in ten minutes. The manager says: “You're all in order, have a nice evening.”
The guard asks to borrow a book for the night shift. He's tired of radio stories about the company's success.
Writing tomorrow's to-do list, there are more “do” items than “rescue” items for the first time.
Your family proposes one gadget-free dinner a week. Your phone seems to object.
The engineer texts that the “Kettle of Hope” passed 10,000 boils without a hitch. Signed: “Time for bed.”
The night foreman admits he used to hate night shifts, but now the floor feels “like home.”
Tonight you drink tea from the “Kettle of Hope” and realise it's the best tea you've had all year.
left: Snap a photo for the team

text: Friends invite you to a Friday birthday. For the first time this year you can say yes with no caveats.
At 9 p.m. the dog brings its lead and looks at you hopefully. The bank report is open on the laptop.
The watchman sees you off: “You leave on time now. So it's all sorted?” You think: almost.
Mum texts: “Saw you on the news. You look tired. Eat properly!” Worrying as ever.
right: Send a photo of your plate

text: Sales want a budget for samples for new clients. Every sample is a free kettle.
The lawyer proposes rewriting all supplier contracts in one format. A month's work, then order.
The call centre proposes staying open till 9 p.m. to catch after-work calls. Agents aren't thrilled.
A plant veteran tells the young ones what it was like under the old director. They listen, increasingly alarmed.
left: Ask him for good stories too

text: The engineer wants a kettle with a left-handed grip. About ten percent of buyers are lefties.
At the meeting you notice nobody says “under the old director” anymore. Now they say “last year.”
For the first time in a year, stock empties faster than it fills. The keeper fears “we'll run out of kettles.”
Defects fell to 1%. QC wants to celebrate, quietly: “Don't want to jinx it.”
The CFO suggests restoring staff health insurance, cut three years ago. Pricey, but people have long asked.
The shop chief asks for new chairs in the break room. The old ones remember the very first director.
The bank offers a new expansion loan. Cheap money, but the debt would grow big again.
A dealer from the next region wants to open a branded store under your name at his own expense.
Logistics reports every truck arrived on time for the first time in a year. He can't believe it and is recounting.
Twenty CVs came in for a welder job. A year ago there were none. HR is overwhelmed.
Marketing proposes bringing back radio ads. There's a budget now, a small one.
left: Bring them back for a month

text: You're eating in the canteen and three workers join your table. No reason, just to chat.
The analyst shows that customers refunded in the recall now buy from you twice as often.
The owner asks if he can sit in on your stand-ups. “Just to listen.”
The button supplier offers to design a backlit switch for you. Free, “out of gratitude.”
The developer intern wants to build a warehouse chatbot that tells you where items are.
The chain that didn't pay for four months early this year now pays early. It wants special terms.
Workers suggest putting plants on the floor. They say greenery “helps you breathe.” The ficus is ready to move.
Your deputy suggests you take two weeks off this summer; he'll cover. He's already drafted a plan.
The press team wants a New Year video greeting for staff. The script is three pages.
The chief accountant asks to take on a trainee: “I want to pass it on while I still remember everything.”
Support proposes publishing response times on the site. They're great now, but what if they slip?
The investor offers to invest, now on your terms. You get to choose.
Your assistant suggests repainting your office from grey to something warm. “Grey is for crises,” she says.
For the first time the meeting is about next year's plans, not debts. Everyone's a bit nervous at the novelty.
The head of sales asks to raise next month's target: “We can do it.” You can't remember the last time.
Security reports the intern's pass now opens every door, including yours. The sysadmin says “it just happened.”
right: Leave it, you've nothing to hide

text: The keeper suggests giving the old shelving to staff for their cottages. Sturdy, if a bit wonky.
The engineer wants to patent an improved spring design. Patents are pricey but stop copycats.
An employee who once feared layoffs comes up: “I bought a flat. With a mortgage. Because I believe in the plant.”
right: Promise not to let him down

text: The sysadmin goes on holiday for the first time in two years. His handover note has one line: “Don't panic.”
left: Pin the note to the wall

text: A shopper at the brand store asks for “that kettle that won't open.” He means the apology edition.
You wake at 7:00 without an alarm and feel rested. It's so unfamiliar it's almost alarming.
A new guard stops you at the gate: “And who are you?” The old guard laughs from the booth: “That's our rescuer.”
The CFO shows the morning forecast: next year salaries can rise 7%. He's in shock himself.
Morning inbox: 40 emails, not one marked “URGENT.” One is titled “Just thanks.”
The intern you kept a year ago runs stand-up for the first time today. He's nervous.
The warehouse no longer needs the old guest dining room: the recalled kettles have finally been recycled.
left: Make it a dining room again
right: Turn it into a training room

text: The logistics head returns from parental leave with a photo of his baby beside your kettle. “The first sound he recognised.”
right: Send it to the press team

text: It's Saturday, but the alarm goes off at six out of habit. You lie there realising you don't have to go anywhere.
Petrovich proposes you play chess against the warehouse keeper “for the plant championship.”
The shareholders send an invitation to the annual meeting marked “Relaxed.”
The courier who brought three boxes of unpaid bills a year ago brings nothing today. He just stopped by to say hi.
It's a cold morning, and for the first time this year you notice how lovely the plant looks in frost.
left: Snap a photo for the chat

text: Accounting asks if they can hang that first statement, the one with a thousand more coming in than going out, in the hallway.
HR proposes a mentoring day: veterans teach newcomers. The floor would slow for half a day.
A new employee asks whether the plant really nearly closed a year ago. He can't believe it.
The engineer has a new idea: a kettle that reminds you to take a break if you switch it on too often.
right: Give the first one to you

text: Your neighbour greets you every morning: “So, kettles boiling?” These days you answer “they are.”
Your assistant asks whether to keep the daily “DO NOT TOUCH” hour. It's caught on.
Marketing pitches a new slogan: “Luchik: Boiling Again.” Sales already ordered T-shirts.
The chief accountant says she's sleeping without ledger dreams for the first time in years. She dreamed of the sea.
The guard reminds you: a year ago today he wouldn't let you in. Today he brought you a pastry.
You're finishing the annual report. Under “Layoffs” you want to write a single word: “None.”
Before the holidays the watchman offers one last game of backgammon. He'll go easy if you're losing.
Someone posts a day-one photo: you holding the “Everything Is Bad” folder. Caption: “Look how it was.”
The chief accountant is staying late, not for reports: she's baking a Friday cake with her team in the office kitchen.
The CFO proposes hiring a second analyst next year. For once there's money for it.
A message from the company's former director: “I read about you. You did what I couldn't. Thank you.”
The last shift before the holidays is over. The foremen left a kettle with a bow on your desk: “From the floor.”
Last meeting of the year. The CFO suggests ending it in five minutes, “a first in history.”
Your family asks what you want for the holiday dinner. For the first time all year, you just want soup.
Your pillow is delighted: bed at 10:30 p.m. The debt spreadsheet is silent. It has nothing left to tell you.
Logistics reports the year's last truck delivered. The driver asks to pass on “thanks for a sane schedule.”
Marketing sends the year-in-review video: shop-floor footage, smiles, the ficus. You've watched it three times.
At the year's last session your coach asks what you'd do differently. You answer honestly: “Start resting sooner.”
The cat sits on your laptop, blocking an email from the bank titled “All in order.”
Staff jokingly present you with a certificate: “Most Patient Boss of the Year.” Signed by the whole plant.
Your sister calls: “So, did you save them?” For the first time you answer: “Yes. We did.”
The keeper calls: “All the kettles have shipped. The warehouse is empty. Is that good or bad?”
The intern asks if next year he can do “something crisis-related” too. You smile.
The shop chief writes: “A year ago I thought you were just another one. I was wrong.” No emojis, which says a lot.
You put the kettle on, sit by the window and plan nothing for the first time in a year. The kettle boils. Very quietly.
The owner sends a holiday note: “Take two weeks off. That's an order.” First order you've been glad to get.
